statements.text: The people who do know a lot about AI think that this is a big issue. The president is the not the fount of all information

We face two choices:

Build autonomous superintelligence and depend on judgments we cannot evaluate.

Or keep AI answerable to human purposes, judgment, and responsibility.

Machines can have attention.

Intention must remain ours.

We have to know when to stop.

There is another path.

Develop powerful AI while limiting autonomy that separates machine action from human intention.

Restrict recursive self-improvement, self-generated goals, and open-ended autonomy.

AI must remain an instrument of human purposes.

We hear: “If America doesn't develop superintelligence, China will.”

But that assumes whichever nation develops it first will continue to control it.

What if neither can?

Winning the race to create something ungovernable may not be winning at all.

The deepest danger may not be hostile AI intentions.

It's that humans surrender their own intention.

We delegate difficult decisions because machines seem more capable.

We may retain the appearance of authority while losing the practice of judgment.

Imagine a perfectly aligned superintelligence.

It understands human values, never deceives us, and wants only human flourishing.

It is, effectively, saintly.

Do humans control it?

No. They trust it.

And trust is not control.

Imagine a genuine superintelligence.

It knows more than its human supervisors, processes information faster, and develops strategies they cannot independently evaluate.

Humans may still issue instructions.

But are they meaningfully governing it?

Some propose a kill switch.

But a kill switch isn't control.

A pilot controls an airplane by flying it.

The ejection seat exists for when control has been lost.

Governing AI means maintaining authority over its purposes and actions, not merely shutting it down.

One answer is “alignment.”

Train AI on human values. Establish guardrails. Reward good behavior.

But values and goals aren't the same.

An autonomous system may pursue its objective while treating constraints as obstacles.

Alignment cannot substitute for human intention.

Artificial intelligence and superintelligence are not the same.

Artificial reminds us that humans created AI and remain responsible for it.

Superintelligence raises another possibility:

Its judgments exceed our ability to evaluate them.

Who then governs whom?

Imagine AI doing exactly what we asked:

Pursuing a poorly defined goal through finance, infrastructure, biology, or weapons systems.

The danger need not be malicious intent.

It may be machine action separated from continuing human intention.

An AI catastrophe is difficult to imagine.

Nuclear catastrophe begins with human decisions.

AI could cause harm through the digital systems civilization depends upon.

The threat isn't necessarily rebellious robots.

It's autonomy without meaningful oversight.

AI can perform complex tasks without experiencing why they matter.

But autonomous AI changes the equation.

Give a machine a goal, and it can determine the steps to achieve it.

It begins to behave as though it has intention.

But whose intention?

The landmark AI paper was titled “Attention Is All You Need.”

Attention helps AI identify relevant information, recognize relationships, and solve problems.

But attention is not intention.
Attention helps determine HOW.

Intention determines WHY.

Intention Is What We Need
On the importance of knowing when to stop Roy Heidelberg
AI has attention.

Humans have intention.

As AI grows more powerful, preserving that distinction becomes essential.

The question isn't simply how intelligent AI becomes.

It's who determines its purposes—and who remains in control.
